findings.issue_text: `parseRefreshTokenResponse` return value (a zod `safeParse` result wrapper) is written directly into `prisma.credential.update({ data: { key } })` in googlecalendar CalendarService.ts:97, persisting `{success: true, data: {...}}` as the credential key and corrupting Google credentials; must use `.data`

In parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts:8-10 the computed keys `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]` both evaluate to the literal string `"[object Object]"`, so the second key overwrites the first and the intended numeric-expiry validation does not exist, letting a response with no expiry pass and causing permanent re-refresh loops

parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts:25-27 injects the literal placeholder string `"refresh_token"` when the response has no refresh_token, which is then spread over existing credentials in office365calendar CalendarService.ts:262, overwriting the real refresh token and permanently breaking refresh until the user reconnects

refreshOAuthTokens.ts:8-15 returns a raw fetch `Response` in sync mode while callers expect provider-shaped values (googlecalendar reads `res?.data`, hubspot casts to `HubspotToken` and reads `.expiresIn`, zoho-bigin/zohocrm read `tokenInfo.data.error`), breaking refresh at runtime while still type-checking due to the `HubspotToken` assertion and `() => any`

zoho-bigin CalendarService.ts:93 passes `credentialId` as the third argument to `refreshOAuthTokens`, which expects `userId`, so the sync endpoint is called with the wrong `calcomUserId` and tokens are fetched for the wrong or nonexistent user

apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts:24-29 compares the webhook secret with `!==`, a non-constant-time comparison on an attacker-supplied header; should use `crypto.timingSafeEqual` on equal-length buffers

packages/lib/constants.ts:103 assigns `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED` the result of `process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET && process.env.CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY`, so its runtime value is the encryption key string rather than a boolean, risking secret leakage into HTML via client-shared/SSR paths; should wrap in `!!(...)`

app-credential.ts:31 uses `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)`, which throws on a malformed body and produces an unhandled rejection/500 with a stack trace instead of a 400; should use `safeParse` and return a validation error

app-credential.ts:55-57 leaves `symmetricDecrypt(...)` and `JSON.parse(...)` unguarded (wrong key, tampered ciphertext, or non-JSON plaintext throws a 500) and never validates that the result is an object, so a scalar can be passed to Prisma's `key` field

app-credential.ts:60-68 uses `prisma.credential.findFirst({ where: { userId, appId } })`, which picks an arbitrary row when a user has multiple credentials for the same app, silently overwriting the wrong account's tokens; the request schema has no disambiguator

app-credential.ts:70-80 update path sets only `key` and never clears the `invalid` flag, so a previously invalid credential stays flagged after fresh keys are synced and the user keeps seeing the broken-app banner

salesforce CalendarService.ts:87 uses `if (response.statusText !== "OK")` as a success check, which is unreliable since `statusText` is empty for HTTP/2 responses (undici) and not normalized, causing every refresh to throw `HttpError` with an empty message; should use `response.ok`/`response.status`

salesforce CalendarService.ts:75-100 runs the refresh POST plus a `prisma.credential.update` unconditionally on every service construction with no expiry check, adding a network round-trip and DB write to every Salesforce operation and risking token-endpoint rate limits

salesforce CalendarService.ts:89 calls `parseRefreshTokenResponse` (which switches to the minimal schema when sync is enabled) but never calls `refreshOAuthTokens`, so with credential sharing on it hits Salesforce directly while skipping its own schema validation; it is the only app not routed through the sync helper

refreshOAuthTokens.ts:8-14 POSTs to `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` with no shared secret, signature, or auth header (only `calcomUserId` and `appSlug`), so the self-hoster's endpoint cannot authenticate the caller and anyone who can reach it can mint access tokens for arbitrary users

refreshOAuthTokens.ts:8-15 has no `response.ok` check and no try/catch around the sync fetch, so a 4xx/5xx from the sync endpoint is returned as a normal response and surfaces later as an opaque parse/`undefined` error inside each app's refresh code

app-credential.ts:25 reads `req.headers[process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME]` without lowercasing, so the lookup never matches if the operator configures the header name with uppercase letters (Node lowercases incoming header keys); the requirement exists only as a comment in `.env.example`
app-credential.ts:17 handler accepts any HTTP method, so a `GET` with the right header performs credential writes; non-`POST` requests should be rejected

goldens.comment: The parseRefreshTokenResponse function incorrectly sets refresh_token to the hardcoded string 'refresh_token' when it's missing from the OAuth refresh token response. This invalidates the token, breaking subsequent token refreshes and causing authentication failures.

The Zod schema in parseRefreshTokenResponse uses computed property keys [z.string().toString()] and [z.string().optional().toString()] in minimumTokenResponseSchema, which is invalid Zod syntax and will throw a runtime error.

parseRefreshTokenResponse returns a Zod safeParse result ({ success, data, error }), not the credential key object. Persisting that as key stores the wrapper instead of the token payload; we should store the parsed data or use schema parse.

When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set, the refreshFunction helper returns the fetch Response, but several callers (for example GoogleCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting res.data, and HubspotCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting a HubspotToken) assume it returns the integration-specific token object. That mismatch will cause runtime errors in the sync-enabled path unless the return type or those call sites are adjusted.

When the sync endpoint path is used, res is a fetch Response and has no .data; res?.data will be undefined and token.access_token will throw at runtime. This relies on a consistent return shape from refreshOAuthTokens, which isn’t guaranteed currently.

The `refreshOAuthTokens` function is passed `credentialId` instead of `userId`, which breaks the credential sync functionality by causing incorrect user lookups. This issue can lead to failures in syncing user credentials, impacting user experience.

The Salesforce integration checks `response.statusText` instead of `response.ok` when handling OAuth token refresh responses. This can lead to unreliable behavior, as a successful response may not be correctly identified, resulting in the use of stale credentials and potential authentication failures.

The `jsforce.Connection` is created using stale `credentialKey.access_token` and `credentialKey.instance_url` after a token refresh, which can lead to authentication failures and incorrect data access. Ensure that the connection is established using the refreshed token values instead.

The `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse` function can throw on invalid payloads, resulting in 500 Internal Server Errors instead of the expected 400 Bad Request responses. This can lead to confusion for clients and hinder proper error handling.

adjudication_records.issue_text: apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts:24-29 compares the webhook secret with `!==`, a non-constant-time comparison on an attacker-supplied header; should use `crypto.timingSafeEqual` on equal-length buffers

adjudication.rationale:
The new webhook handler in `apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts` validates the secret via a direct inequality check:

```ts
req.headers[process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME || "calcom-webhook-secret"] !== process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET
```

This is a normal JavaScript string/primitive comparison against attacker-controlled input (the request header). Such comparisons are not constant-time and can theoretically leak information via timing differences. Using `crypto.timingSafeEqual` (after normalizing to Buffers and checking equal length) is the standard mitigation for secret comparisons. The finding accurately describes what is present in the diff and is a legitimate security concern introduced by this new endpoint.

adjudication.rationale: In the new `apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts`, the handler does `const keys = JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(reqBody.keys, process.env.CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY || ""));` with no try/catch and no validation of the decrypted/parsed value. If the env key is missing/incorrect, ciphertext is tampered, or plaintext isn’t valid JSON, `symmetricDecrypt(...)` and/or `JSON.parse(...)` will throw and the API route will return an unhandled 500. Also, `JSON.parse` can legitimately return non-object JSON (string/number/boolean/null/array), and that value is passed directly to Prisma as `data: { key: keys }`, so there is no guarantee `key` is an object-shaped credential payload.

adjudication.rationale: The new webhook handler looks up an existing credential with `prisma.credential.findFirst({ where: { userId: reqBody.userId, appId: appMetadata.slug } })` and then updates that single row. `findFirst` has no deterministic ordering and the code provides no disambiguator (e.g., credential id / external account id) in the request schema, so if a user has more than one `credential` row for the same `appId` (which is plausible here because the code explicitly comments it can’t use `upsert` “as we don't know the id of the credential”, implying no unique constraint on (userId, appId)), the endpoint may update an arbitrary matching credential and overwrite the wrong account’s keys.

adjudication_records.issue_text: refreshOAuthTokens.ts:8-15 has no `response.ok` check and no try/catch around the sync fetch, so a 4xx/5xx from the sync endpoint is returned as a normal response and surfaces later as an opaque parse/`undefined` error inside each app's refresh code

adjudication.rationale: Yes. In `packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/refreshOAuthTokens.ts` the sync-path does `await fetch(...)` and immediately `return response;` without checking `response.ok` or handling non-2xx/error bodies. Several callers then assume a successful token shape (e.g., Google reads `res?.data`, Hubspot types it as `HubspotToken`, etc.), so a 4xx/5xx from the sync endpoint would propagate as a normal `Response` and likely fail later with confusing/opaque errors rather than being rejected at the boundary.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app-credential.ts:25 reads `req.headers[process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME]` without lowercasing, so the lookup never matches if the operator configures the header name with uppercase letters (Node lowercases incoming header keys); the requirement exists only as a comment in `.env.example`

adjudication.rationale: In apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts the secret check indexes req.headers with the exact string from process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME (or the default). In Node/Next, incoming header names are normalized to lowercase keys on req.headers, so if an operator sets CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME to a mixed/uppercase value (e.g. "X-Calcom-Webhook-Secret"), req.headers["X-Calcom-Webhook-Secret"] will be undefined and the comparison will fail, causing an erroneous 403. The only safeguard is a comment in .env.example (“Should be in lowercase”), not an enforced lowercasing in code, so the defect is present in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app-credential.ts:17 handler accepts any HTTP method, so a `GET` with the right header performs credential writes; non-`POST` requests should be rejected

adjudication.rationale: In `apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts`, the exported Next.js API `handler` never checks `req.method` before parsing `req.body` and performing Prisma `update`/`create` writes. That means any HTTP method (including GET) that supplies a body and the correct secret header can reach the credential write logic. This is directly verifiable from the diff: there is no `if (req.method !== "POST") ...` guard, yet the handler mutates the database unconditionally after auth checks.

adjudication_records.issue_text: office365calendar CalendarService.ts:262 removes the only `console.error` diagnostic for a failed Outlook token parse while `parseRefreshTokenResponse` now throws instead of degrading gracefully, leaving the remaining `tokenResponse.success && tokenResponse.data` guard as dead code and making refresh failures less debuggable

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `Office365CalendarService` changed from `refreshTokenResponseSchema.safeParse(responseJson)` with an explicit `console.error(...)` on failure, to `parseRefreshTokenResponse(responseJson, refreshTokenResponseSchema)`. The new `parseRefreshTokenResponse` uses `safeParse` internally but immediately `throw new Error("Invalid refreshed tokens were returned")` when `success` is false, so the old non-throwing behavior + diagnostic logging is removed. Because it throws on any parse failure, the subsequent `tokenResponse.success && tokenResponse.data` spread in `o365AuthCredentials = { ...o365AuthCredentials, ...(tokenResponse.success && tokenResponse.data) };` becomes effectively unreachable for the failure case (i.e., dead/pointless guard). The thrown error also drops the previous detailed logging of the zod error and MS response, making failures harder to debug based on the code in the diff.
